method.value: Reduce Keck images, Richardson-Lucy deconvolve, align disks and subtract median disk emission

evidence.quote: Reduction steps included median sky subtraction, application of a flat field, construction of a bad pixel map and subsequent bad pixel removal, cosmic ray removal, and flux calibration using the photometric standard stars.
For image deconvolution, we used the richardson_lucy function from the skimage.restoration image restoration module by Scikit-Image (cite: van_der_walt_scikit-image_2014).

we determined the median disk emission (calculated from the reduced, deconvolved, and stacked frames) and subtracted it from all of the frames so that only refracted starlight along the limb was visible in each frame.

key_parameters.value: Universal PSF from the frame with the sharpest star

evidence.quote: We ultimately used a universal PSF derived from the frame with the sharpest star, as this gave the sharpest deconvolved disks.

key_parameters.value: Fit a circle to minimum radial gradients; align fitted disk centers

evidence.quote: Then, a circle was fit to the minimum radial gradient values for all angles around the circle
the images were then aligned so that the (x,y) coordinates of the center of the fitted circles were stacked on top of each other.

validation.value: Compare PSFs on pre- and post-occultation frames; choose the sharpest deconvolved disks

evidence.quote: To find the best PSF for deconvolution, we studied the effectiveness of different PSFs in frames before and after occultation, when the occulted star was in the frame alongside Titan.
We ultimately used a universal PSF derived from the frame with the sharpest star, as this gave the sharpest deconvolved disks.

evidence.quote: Two one-dimensional Gaussians led to centroids with the least variability.
Titan-star offsets were calculated for all pre- and post-occultation frames by taking the difference of the star centroid and the fitted circle center for Titan’s disk.
Linear fits were applied to both the x- and y- directions (as a function of time) in order to interpolate the x- and y-offsets during the frames when the star was not visible

method.value: Simultaneously fit eight CH3CN lines with Moffat functions in every image pixel

evidence.quote: The Gaussian line fitting method was updated to use the Moffat function (cite: moffat1969theoretical) instead

All eight CH$_3$CN spectral lines were fitted simultaneously for all pixels in the ALMA images, using a Levenberg-Marquardt least-squares minimization routine written in Python, based on the MPFIT package (cite: markwardt2009non).

key_parameters.value: Common variable velocity offset across all lines; other Moffat parameters independent for each line

evidence.quote: All parameters of the Moffat function were allowed to vary independently for each line, apart from the velocity offset parameter, for which a common (variable) value was used for all lines.

fitting.value: Levenberg-Marquardt least squares; Doppler uncertainties from covariance-matrix diagonal elements

evidence.quote: using a Levenberg-Marquardt least-squares minimization routine written in Python, based on the MPFIT package (cite: markwardt2009non).
The uncertainty on the Doppler shift for each pixel was derived from the diagonal elements of the covariance matrix.

validation.value: Moffat functions reproduce observed line profiles within the noise

evidence.quote: We found that the Moffat function was able to fully reproduce our observed line profiles (within the noise), resulting in a more accurate determination of the line Doppler shift than the conventional Gaussian fitting method.

method.value: Average fitted line-of-sight velocities inside Titan’s limb and subtract the resulting zero-point shift from individual pixels

evidence.quote: The magnitude of the shift was calculated by taking the average of the fitted line-of-sight velocities inside Titan’s limb.
This “zero point shift” was then subtracted from the individual pixel Doppler shifts for the subsequent data analysis steps.

key_parameters.value: Approximately +30 m s^-1 offset

evidence.quote: A significant ($\approx+30$ m s$^{-1}$) offset in the spectral line Doppler shifts was identified at the center of Titan’s disk (and along the direction of its polar axis).

method.value: NEMESIS radiative transfer and CH3CN abundance retrieval; derive wind contribution from altitude functional derivatives weighted by the spectral-line gradient

evidence.quote: we used the Non-linear optimal Estimator for MultivariatE spectral analySIS (NEMESIS) to generate a detailed radiative transfer model for the observed CH$_3$CN emission

This abundance profile formed the basis of our “wind contribution function” calculation, which was obtained from the corresponding NEMESIS functional derivatives ($dQ/dz$) of flux with respect to altitude, as a function of frequency.

The $dQ/dz$ values were convolved with the gradient of the (continuum-subtracted) model spectral line profile, to provide weighting according to the frequencies contributing most to the retrieved line Doppler shifts

method.value: Fit a simplified 3D radiative transfer Doppler map with modified atmWindMapGaussFit to account for beam-smearing and axial tilt

evidence.quote: Due to the effects of beam-smearing, combined with Titan’s axial tilt, extraction of the intrinsic zonal wind field requires deconvolution of the Doppler shift data.
We therefore followed a similar method to (cite: cordiner_detection_2020) to model the Doppler map and extract a latitudinal wind speed profile using a simplified 3D radiative transfer model.

The `atmWindMapGaussFit` code of (cite: cordiner_detection_2020) was modified to allow a continuously variable wind speed as a function of latitude ($v(l)$), instead of the Gaussian profile previously assumed by those authors.

key_parameters.value: Segmented linear interpolation, smoothed with Gaussian FWHM equal to point spacing

evidence.quote: by a segmented linear function. This function was then smoothed by a Gaussian function of FWHM equal to the spacing between the points.

key_parameters.value: Exponential taper with 1 degree scale length; zero wind at poles

evidence.quote: An exponential taper was applied at the ends of the $v(l)$ profile (with an exponential smoothing scale length of 1$^{\circ}$), to ensure a velocity of zero at the poles.

validation.value: Experiment with point counts; seven points give a good Doppler-map fit while remaining constrained by the data

evidence.quote: To maximize the information content in the $v(l)$ retrieval, we experimented in fitting the observations with profiles incorporating different numbers of variable latitudinal points $i$.

Seven latitudinal points (with $\Delta{(l)}=30^{\circ}$ separation) were found to produce a good fit to the observed Doppler map, while still allowing the retrieved profile to be well constrained by the data

referee_caveats_inferred: The approximate Doppler zero-point correction has no stated uncertainty propagation into the retrieved wind profile.
Angular SSE ranks models without a stated error-weighted likelihood or significance test.
The preferred original-amplitude profile differs from the preferred profile across all tested amplitudes; answer keys must distinguish those searches.
Table 2 reports 29.0 for doubled L_s 240-degree ingress SSE, whereas Table 4 reports 28.9.
The 303 km average emission altitude, contribution-function peak reference and 307 km GCM reference should not be treated as interchangeable.
Failure at mid-event limits interpretation of the best-ranked profile as a complete atmospheric solution.
The source of the specific 8.94 au ALMA plotting distance is not explicitly identified.
